module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 50

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/50](https://www.erdosproblems.com/50)
* [Er95] Erdős, Paul, Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and geometry.
Resenhas (1995), 165-186.
* [Sch38] Schoenberg, I. J. "On asymptotic distributions of arithmetical functions."
Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 39.2 (1936): 315-330.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Set MeasureTheory Topology
open scoped Nat Topology

namespace Erdos50

/--
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is the asymptotic distribution function of the values
of $\varphi(n)/n$ if for all $c \in [0, 1]$, the natural density of $\{n : \varphi(n) < cn\}$
exists and equals $f(c)$.
-/
def IsDistributionOfPhiRatio (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ c ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, {n : ℕ | (φ n : ℝ) < c * n}.HasDensity (f c)

/--
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is purely singular (or singular continuous) on a set
$s \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ if it is continuous on $s$ and its derivative within $s$ equals zero
almost everywhere on $s$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.
-/
def IsPurelySingularOn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (s : Set ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContinuousOn f s ∧ ∀ᵐ x ∂(volume.restrict s), derivWithin f s x = 0

/--
Schoenberg [Sch38] proved that the asymptotic distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$ exists.
That is, for any $c \in [0, 1]$, the proportion of integers $n \le N$ satisfying $\varphi(n)/n < c$
approaches a limit as $N \to \infty$. This limit function is the cumulative distribution function
of the values of $\varphi(n)/n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50_schoenberg : ∃ f : ℝ → ℝ, IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős [Er95] proved that the distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$ is purely singular on
$[0, 1]$: it is continuous there, but its derivative is zero almost everywhere on $[0, 1]$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50_singular (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f) :
    IsPurelySingularOn f (Icc 0 1) := by
  sorry

/--
Let $f$ be the asymptotic distribution function of $\varphi(n)/n$, so that for each $c \in [0,1]$,
$f(c)$ is the natural density of $\{n : \varphi(n) < cn\}$. Is it true that there is no $x$ such
that the derivative $f'(x)$ exists and is positive?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_50 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f),
    ¬∃ x ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, ∃ y > 0, HasDerivWithinAt f y (Icc 0 1) x := by
  sorry

end Erdos50

findings.description: The module docstring cites "[Sch38] Schoenberg, I. J. 'On asymptotic distributions of arithmetical functions.' Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 39.2 (1936): 315-330", and the docstring of `erdos_50_schoenberg` also says "Schoenberg [Sch38]". The label points to 1938, but the cited paper appeared in 1936, so the label and the year disagree. The label does not come from erdosproblems.com, which cites no Schoenberg paper for #50. This is a pure citation slip. No statement is affected.
findings.source_evidence: Crossref record for DOI 10.1090/s0002-9947-1936-1501849-x: Schoenberg, "On asymptotic distributions of arithmetical functions", Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 39, issue 2, pp. 315-330, published-print 1936 (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/s0002-9947-1936-1501849-x). erdosproblems.com/50 (Wayback snapshot 2026-07-09) says only "Schoenberg proved that ..." and lists [Er95] as its reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename the label to [Sch36] in the module docstring and in the docstring of `erdos_50_schoenberg`. Alternatively, if Schoenberg's original φ(n)/n result was meant, cite his 1928 Math. Z. 28 paper as [Sch28].

reformulations.difference: The source talks about "the" density function f(c), defined for c ∈ [0,1], and asks whether no x has f'(x) existing and positive. The Lean statement quantifies over every f : ℝ → ℝ that equals the density on [0,1]; values outside [0,1] are unconstrained. It restricts x to Icc 0 1 and uses `HasDerivWithinAt f y (Icc 0 1) x`, which is a one-sided derivative at the endpoints 0 and 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (a) Such an f exists (Schoenberg; this is `erdos_50_schoenberg`), and any two such f agree on [0,1] because limits are unique (proved in scratch). `HasDerivWithinAt f y (Icc 0 1) x` for x ∈ [0,1] depends only on f restricted to [0,1] (proved). Given existence, the `∀ f, hf → ...` form is therefore equivalent to the `∃ f, hf ∧ ...` form ("the f") (proved). (b) For x ∈ (0,1), `HasDerivWithinAt f y (Icc 0 1) x ↔ HasDerivAt f y x` (proved). (c) The endpoints never give a finite positive derivative. At 0: f(0) = 0 (proved), and Markov with the finite mean M₂ of (n/φ(n))² gives f(c) ≤ M₂c². So the derivative within [0,1] at 0 is 0, and it is unique (proved); y > 0 is impossible. At 1: f(1) = 1, and 1 − f(1−ε) = d{n : φ(n)/n ≥ 1−ε} ≫ 1/log(1/ε), because (1/ε)-rough numbers have density about e^{-γ}/log(1/ε) and most of them satisfy Σ_{p|n} 1/p ≤ ε. So the left difference quotient at 1 tends to +∞ and no finite derivative within [0,1] exists there. A totient sieve up to 3·10⁶ agrees: f(0.2)/0.2 ≈ 7·10⁻⁴, while (1−f(1−ε))/ε grows 1.3, 2.1, 3.3, 6.8, 11.9, 20.6, 41.2, 72.3 for ε = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.002, 0.001. Given these two endpoint facts, I proved in Lean that the RHS is equivalent to "for all f with hf, no x ∈ (0,1) and y > 0 with HasDerivAt f y x". That is exactly the source's question. The conclusion is the same if f is extended to ℝ by the same density formula (0 on (−∞,0], 1 on [1,∞)). The derivative must be finite: if +∞ were allowed, the answer would trivially be "no", since a monotone singular function has f' = +∞ on a set of full μ_f-measure. The polarity matches: answer True means "yes, there is no such x".

reformulations.difference: `IsPurelySingularOn f s` is `ContinuousOn f s ∧ ∀ᵐ x ∂(volume.restrict s), derivWithin f s x = 0`. Mathlib's `derivWithin` returns 0 wherever f is not differentiable, and the definition does not require monotonicity or bounded variation. As a general definition it is therefore weaker than "singular continuous": for example, a continuous nowhere-differentiable function satisfies it.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: In `erdos_50_singular` the definition is applied only to an f satisfying `IsDistributionOfPhiRatio f`. Such an f is monotone on [0,1]; I proved this from `Set.HasDensity.mono`, since the sets {n : φ(n) < cn} are nested. By Lebesgue's theorem (`MonotoneOn.ae_differentiableWithinAt`), f is differentiable within [0,1] almost everywhere. I proved in Lean that for every f satisfying the hypothesis, `IsPurelySingularOn f (Icc 0 1)` is equivalent to `ContinuousOn f (Icc 0 1) ∧ ∀ᵐ x ∂(volume.restrict (Icc 0 1)), HasDerivWithinAt f 0 (Icc 0 1) x`. So the junk value never matters here. For a monotone function, continuity plus f' = 0 a.e. means the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure has no atoms and is singular (Lebesgue decomposition), i.e. it is purely singular. That is the result Erdős proved (Amer. J. Math. 61 (1939), §3, applied to log(φ(n)/n)), and it is what erdosproblems.com's remark states.

review.notes:
I found no misformalization. All three theorems match erdosproblems.com/50 as posed: \"Schoenberg proved that for every c∈[0,1] the density of {n : φ(n)<cn} exists. Let this density be denoted by f(c). Is it true that there are no x such that f'(x) exists and is positive?\" The remark reads \"Erdős [Er95] could prove the distribution function is purely singular.\" The statement is identical in the snapshots of 2025-09-14 and 2026-07-09. The problem is still OPEN ($250) there and in the teorth/erdosproblems database, so the `research open` tag is current. The two solved variants are correctly tagged `research solved`.

Checks done:
- `Set.HasDensity` is the standard natural density (#(S ∩ [0,b)) / b → α).
- `answer(sorry)` defaults to `True` (repository convention). The right-hand side is the positive form of the question, so this is not a negated conjecture.
- All quantifiers sit inside the RHS.
- `IsDistributionOfPhiRatio` is satisfiable (Schoenberg), so the `∀ f` form is not vacuous.
- Proved in scratch files: f(0) = 0; the set at c = 1 is {n ≥ 2}, so f(1) = 1; f is unique and monotone on [0,1]; interior and endpoint derivative facts; the conditional reduction to the interior, two-sided question; the equivalence of `IsPurelySingularOn` with a form that avoids the `derivWithin` junk value.

Optional reference improvement, not a defect relative to the cited source: the docstring of `erdos_50_singular` says \"Erdős [Er95] proved\", following erdosproblems.com. The actual proof is in Erdős, \"On the smoothness of the asymptotic distribution of additive arithmetical functions\", Amer. J. Math. 61 (1939) 722–725. I confirmed this from the OCR text: §3 shows the distribution of log(φ(n)/n) is not absolutely continuous and hence, by Jessen–Wintner, purely singular.

I could not read the primary text [Er95, p.171] (Resenhas IME-USP 1995); it is not online. The review relies on erdosproblems.com's statement, which is the cited source. The live erdosproblems.com site blocks curl, so I read it through Wayback snapshots.
